Side effects in function composition
How to add a side effect to a JavaScript function composition without breaking the chain: tap for logging pipe steps and for actions the program needs.
Learn to add side effects to a function composition, such as logging for debugging or actions the program logic requires, so that the data keeps flowing down the chain unchanged.
text

Based on the principles of functional programming, one might think that creating side effects within function composition is forbidden. But in reality, any program, and especially web development, will create some side effect no matter what (DOM operations, input/output operations, logging, and so on ...).
In real-world cases, side effects within function composition can be useful to us mainly in two situations:
list
Debugging the composition and logging it, in case of errors or simply to understand the execution flow and how the input data changes within the function composition.
Creating a side effect within the program according to its logic and continuing the execution of the function composition.
Let's try to inspect the intermediate results within a function composition by creating a side effect in the form of logging the data.
code
But how do we obtain the results of each function call in pipeline (prop ('money') ...), if there won't even be any errors in the composition and we simply want to debug the code.
Let's write a universal utility for any case in the chain of composition calls.
previous-block
Any program, and especially web development, creates side effects: DOM operations, input and output, logging.
In function composition, side effects are needed mainly in two cases: for debugging and logging, and for actions the program logic requires, after which the composition keeps running.
The tap :: (a -> *) -> a -> a utility calls the given function with the argument and returns that same argument, so the next function in the composition receives the data unchanged.
A logger built as tap (console.log) and placed between the steps of pipe prints the intermediate result after each call.

To debug the total pipeline, someone put console.log straight between its steps, and the pipeline broke: console.log returns undefined, and the next step receives it instead of the data. Write tap and a labelled logger tapLog :: String -> a -> a that prints the line "label: value" (the value via JSON.stringify) and returns its argument unchanged. Put tapLog after each step of total instead of console.log, with the labels "items", "sum" and "discounted".

items: [40,20,50]
sum: 110
discounted: 100
100

The second case is a side effect the program logic requires. Write tapWhen :: (a -> Boolean) -> (a -> *) -> a -> a: it calls the effect function only if the predicate returned true, and returns the argument in any case. Use it at the start of the checkout pipeline to add the user's name to the declined log when they don't have enough money for the product. The composition must still run to the end and return a message.

the product can be purchased
you don't have enough money
the product can be purchased
not enough money: Anna
